***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Nàjqwea has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "cowàp zbuamey" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Nàjqwea into English.

*****
NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Nàjqwea nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: cowàp "king", cowàvwày "kings". A few nouns, called monàmecojnàwej qjaqmewu ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. cujyqcoj "a camp", nàweqqwàcojwà "a letter", amemoqwejwà "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    wemoywà cowàp "the king himself" (masculine)
    wemoyj cowàvweaj "the queen herself" (feminine)
    wemoymewu zwànànàmewu "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as xebuwuweamey "master", momewàco "boy", xewàmey "god", but also some inanimate objects such as sebucoqmey "garden", wàpwàcocuweqmey "army", wubuy "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -mey or -wàco are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as momewànànàj "girl", wumenàwewàco "woman", xewàj "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as jcozbuco "tree", mecozy "city", semewujaweqjy "kindness", ajqwebu "nation". Words in the 1st declension like momewànànàj ending in -j are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as mobuwàqj "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -qjy and -qwebu.
    Neuter nouns (apart from ycubucoqmewu "a sex worker (of either gender)") all refer to things, such as abuwuwàa "name", cubucomomey "body", zwànànàmewu "war", fwàawàamewu 'poison'.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of neuter nouns is formed by adding the morpheme j, e.g. zwànànàj "wars", cubucomobucoj "bodies"; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical. 

* Case

Nouns in Nàjqwea have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is cowàp when it is the subject of a verb, but cowàvwàwu when it is the object:

    cowàp fwexewàq "the king sees" (nominative case)
    cowàvwàwu fwexewàq "(he/she/it) sees the king" (accusative case)

Further cases mean "of" (genitive case), "to/for" (dative case), and "with" (ablative case).

The genitive, dative and ablative cases are called the "oblique" cases.

The order in which the cases are given in Nàjqwea grammar books differs from one author to the other.

* Use of cases

** Nominative

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

    cowàp xemecuweq = the king leads
    cowàp jmexeweqmeco = the king is heard

It is also used for the complement of a copula verb such as wàyq "he is" or hjcuqmey wàyq "he became":

    cowàp wàcojq jwàawàjy abuzwey = our king was jwàawàjy / jwàawàjy was our king
    cowàp hjcuqmey wàyq = he was made king / he became king

** Vocative

The vocative case is used when addressing someone:

    xomezwàyawà wuwà, cobuwumenàwà cowàp, hbuwàxemey hwàcowecowà? = do you order me, King cobuwumenàmey, to strike a treaty?

** Accusative

The accusative case is used for the object of a sentence:

    mobuwàqjwà cowàvwàwu fwexewàzmeaq = the poets will see the king
    wujnàmey cowàp abufbuy xemecuwày qwewuwàq = the bad king fears the new generals

It is also used as the subject of an infinitival clause dependent on a verb of speaking or the like:

    cowàvwàwu weaqwàcohwàcuqmewu wàyywà cucowàxewàzjaq = they believed that the king had been killed

It can be the complement of another word which is itself accusative:

    qmenànàmewu mobumomenàmey cowàvwàwu cucowàjfweq = the people made qmenànàmey their king

It can also be used with a place name to refer to the destination:

    cobuwuj mocobuhwàcuqmey wàyq = he set out for cobuwuwà

The accusative is also used after various prepositions (especially those that imply motion towards):

    ywàajqmey jxe cowàvwàwu nàwàvjqbuy wuweyweq = the ywàajqwà sent ambassadors to the king
    cubuaymenà wea mecozwàwu cowàxeweweq = the magistrate returned to the city

Another use of the accusative is to give a length of time or distance:

    cowàvajfweq jaabuy rmewearmewà = he reigned for five years
    rmewearmewà mowàxewày nàbuavmey = five foot tall

** Genitive

A genitive noun can represent a possessor or a kin:

    cowàvwey hwenàwej = the king's daughter, daughter of the king
    nàwezcowe momewànànàjwà = the girl's books, the books of the girl

A genitive noun always stands for the object of mental processes such as wuweywàcowàbuco "I pity" and buznàwefweycubuco "I forget" and the accusative is never used with those two verbs:

    mobumomenàmey buznàwefweycuwàqmeco wujnàwe cowàvwey = the nation will forget the bad king
    xemep zbuamey wuweywàcowàqmeco momewàcobucomewu = the good general pities the boys

A genitive noun attached to a verbal noun can stand for the object of the implied verb (called an "objective genitive"):

    wujpwewuwe fwecowe xewàywexewàcowemewu = my longing for the great man

A genitive noun can stand for the subject of the implied verb (called a "subjective" genitive):

    cujwàyjcowey jxefwàaqmey = cujwàyjco's arrival

A frequent type of genitive is the partitive genitive, expressing the quantity of something:

    yjqwey qwàwumobucowey = enough time

** Dative

The dative case means "to" or "for". It is frequently used with verbs of saying or giving:

    cowàvwe ameaqwejqmewu wàyq = it was announced to the king
    mowàcumeawejwu cowàvwe cucowàxewexeweq = he entrusted the money to the king

It can also be used with certain adjectives:

    cujcoweyywewumey wàcojq cowàvwe = he was very dear to the king

It is also used with certain verbs such as mojcowàbu "I obey" or mowàcoymejxewàbu "I persuade":

    mojcomeweq cowàvwe = he was obedient to (i.e. obeyed) the king

There are also various idiomatic uses, such as the dative of possession:

    rmewexe wàyq qwezwe abuwuwàa? = what's your name?

** Ablative

The ablative case can mean "with", especially when the noun it refers to is a thing rather than a person:

    vnàjxewebu ywà qcojayhwevweq = he stabbed himself with a sword

Often a phrase consisting of a noun plus participle in the ablative can express time or circumstance. This is known as an "ablative absolute":

    cowàvwezmey wàpjcuqwey = with the kings driven out, i.e. after the kings were driven out

It is also frequently used with prepositions, especially those meaning "from", "with", "in", or "by":

    meamey wà cowàvwezmey = one from (i.e. one of) the kings
    cumewu cowàvwezmey = with the kings
    j cowàvwezmey = by the kings, from the kings
    mocobu cowàvwà = for/on behalf of the king
    

Another use is in expressions of time and place (except those that give the length of time or distance):

    wàbu qwàwumobucowà = at that time
    sebucu nàbucubu = at this place
    mojmecuwey xewewàzmey = in a few days

The ablative can also mean "from", especially with place names:

    cobuwuj mocobuhwàcuqmey wàyq = he set out from cobuwuwà
    nàbucubu wenànàwà wubuqmey wàyq = he was dislodged from his position

***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Adðiwsij has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "agàgàj xmijruñ" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Adðiwsij into English.

NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Adðiwsij nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: agàgàj "king", agàgeþàguñ "kings". A few nouns, called awadragðadsð iwðijiwrv ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. edðuñiwagð "a camp", adsiwiwàg "a letter", ijrawiwsðàg "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    sawuñàg agàgàj "the king himself" (masculine)
    sawuñð agàgeþsijð "the queen herself" (feminine)
    sawuñrv xàgadadrv "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as kmvsijruñ "master", awràgag "boy", kàgruñ "god", but also some inanimate objects such as ugmagiwruñ "garden", àgàjàgagedsiwruñ "army", vmuñ "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -ruñ or -àgag are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as awràgadadð "girl", vradsàgag "woman", kàgð "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as ðagxmag "tree", ragxuñ "city", ugrvðijsiwðuñ "kindness", ijðiwsm "nation". Words in the 1st declension like awràgadadð ending in -ð are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as awmàgiwð "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -iwðuñ and -iwsm.
    Neuter nouns (apart from uñedmagiwrv "a sex worker (of either gender)") all refer to things, such as ijmvàgij "name", edmagawruñ "body", xàgadadrv "war", èàgijàgijrv 'poison'.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of a neuter noun is formed by adding the morpheme ð; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical.

Nouns in Adðiwsij have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is agàgàj when it is the subject of a verb, but agàgeþàgv when it is the object:

Further cases mean "of" (genitive case), "to/for" (dative case), and "with" (ablative case).

The genitive, dative and ablative cases are called the "oblique" cases.

The order in which the cases are given in Adðiwsij grammar books differs from one author to the other.

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

**********
ADJECTIVES
**********

Adjectives, like nouns, have different endings for the different cases, singular and plural. They also differ as to gender, having different forms for masculine, feminine, and neuter. (But masculine and neuter are identical in the genitive, dative, and ablative cases.) 

Many adjectives belong to the 1st and 2nd declensions, declining in the same way as the nouns þfunyyki, ébsuzimfuge, zunyyfusu. An example is the adjective zubmfuge "good" shown below: 

Case         | Masculine Singular (zubmfuge) | Feminine Singular (zubmki) | Neuter Singular (zubmfusu) | Masculine Plural (zubmzi) | Feminine Plural (zubmkin) | Neuter Plural (zubmki)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Nominative   | zubmfuge                      | zubmki                     | zubmfusu                   | zubmzi                    | zubmkin                   | zubmki
Vocative     | zubmn                       | zubmki                     | zubmfusu                   | zubmzi                    | zubmkin                   | zubmki
Accusative   | zubmfusu                      | zubmkisu                    | zubmfusu                   | zubmbge                   | zubmkige                   | zubmki
Genitive     | zubmzi                       | zubmkin                    | zubmzi                    | zubmbsafusu                 | zubmkisafusu                 | zubmbsafusu
Dative       | zubmb                       | zubmkin                    | zubmb                    | zubmzige                   | zubmzige                   | zubmzige
Ablative     | zubmb                       | zubmki                     | zubmb                    | zubmzige                   | zubmzige                   | zubmzige


    
*****
VERBS
*****

Kèkipzim is a heavily inflected language with largely free word order. Nouns are inflected for number and case; pronouns and adjectives (including participles) are inflected for number, case, and gender; and verbs are inflected for person, number, tense, aspect, voice, and mood. The inflections are often changes in the ending of a word, but can be more complicated, especially with verbs. Thus verbs can take any of over 100 different endings to express different meanings.

* Kèkipzim conjugation

In linguistics and grammar, conjugation has two basic meanings. One meaning is the creation of derived forms of a verb from basic forms, or principal parts.

The second meaning of the word conjugation is a group of verbs which all have the same pattern of inflections. Thus all those Kèkipzim verbs which in the present tense have 1st singular -b, 2nd singular -kige, and infinitive -kisan are said to belong to the 1st conjugation, those with 1st singular -nb, 2nd singular -nge and infinitive -nsan belong to the 2nd conjugation, and so on. The number of conjugations of regular verbs is usually said to be four.

In addition to regular verbs, which belong to one or other of the four regular conjugations, there are also a few irregular verbs, which have a different pattern of endings. The most frequent of these is the verb gefusu, ngegen "to be" together with its prefixed derivatives.

There also exist deponent Kèkipzim verbs, which though active in meaning have endings identical to the passive verbs. Examples in the different conjugations are: (1) subsabsa, subsakisazi "to delay", (2) þbyyzigènbsa, þbyyzigènsazi "to promise", suzigensanbsa, suzigensansazi "to pity" (3) genofubsa, genofuzi "to follow", bzuyzivzigegèbsa, bzuyzivzigegèzi "to forget" and sanfèsanézibsa, sanfèsanézi "to go back", (4) sunmpzibsa, sunmpzisazi "to lie (tell a lie)". Some verbs are semi-deponent, using passive forms for the perfect tenses only. 

* Principal parts

A verb's full paradigm relies on multiple stems. The present indicative active and the present infinitive are both based on the present stem.

It is not possible to infer the stems for other tenses from the present stem. This means that, although the infinitive active form normally shows the verb conjugation, knowledge of several different forms is necessary to be able to confidently produce the full range of forms for any particular verb.

In a dictionary, Kèkipzim verbs are listed with four "principal parts" (or fewer for deponent and defective verbs), which allow the student to deduce the other conjugated forms of the verbs. These are:

    the first person singular of the present indicative active
    the present infinitive active
    the first person singular of the perfect indicative active
    the supine or, in some grammars, the perfect passive participle, which uses the same stem. (Texts that list the perfect passive participle use the future active participle for intransitive verbs.) Some verbs lack this principal part altogether.

**********

* Number

Most Akrudèuw nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: ajiwb "king", ajiwciwo "kings". A few nouns, called éwakçajrakèr udruwudçm ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. ywroudajr "a camp", akèududiwajriw "a letter", uwçéwudèriw "a wedding".

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    èéwoiw ajiwb "the king himself" (masculine)
    èéwor ajiwcèuwr "the queen herself" (feminine)
    èéwoçm éhiwakakçm "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as yhgmèuwço "master", éwçiwaj "boy", yhiwço "god", but also some inanimate objects such as tgajudço "garden", iwbiwajywèudço "army", mgo "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -ço or -iwaj are usually masculine.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of neuter nouns is formed by adding the morpheme r; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical. 

* Case

Nouns in Akrudèuw have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is ajiwb when it is the subject of a verb, but ajiwciwm when it is the object:

    ajiwciwm éfèyhiwud "(he/she/it) leads the king" (accusative case)

Further cases mean "of" (genitive case), "to/for" (dative case), and "with" (ablative case).

The genitive, dative and ablative cases are called the "oblique" cases.

The order in which the cases are given in Akrudèuw grammar books differs from one author to the other.

** Nominative

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

The accusative case is used for the object of a sentence:

**Nouns**

* Number

Most Zoàçoséh nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: nqem "king", nqeleqedé "kings". A few nouns, called rzoynàzoséà çoàhçoyso ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. vàdéçonà "a camp", zoséçoçoqenàqe "a letter", hyrçoséàqe "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    sérdéqe nqem "the king himself" (masculine)
    sérdéà nqeleséhà "the queen herself" (feminine)
    sérdéyso tqezozoyso "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as cjososéhydé "master", ryqen "boy", cqeydé "god", but also some inanimate objects such as sèjonçoydé "garden", qemqenvséçoydé "army", sojodé "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -ydé or -qen are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as ryqezozoà "girl", soyzoséqen "woman", cqeà "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as àntjon "tree", yntdé "city", sèysoàhséçoàdé "kindness", hàçoséjo "nation". Words in the 1st declension like ryqezozoà ending in -à are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as rjoqeçoà "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -çoàdé and -çoséjo.
    Neuter nouns (apart from dévjonçoyso "a sex worker (of either gender)") all refer to things, such as hjosoqeh "name", vjonrydé "body", tqezozoyso "war", pèqehqehyso 'poison'.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of a neuter noun is formed by adding the morpheme à, e.g. hjosoqeh 'name' becomes àhjosoqeh 'names'; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical. 

* Case

Nouns in Zoàçoséh have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is nqem when it is the subject of a verb, but nqeleqeso when it is the object:

** Nominative

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

    nqem àycséço = the king is heard

It is also used for the complement of a copula verb such as qedéço "he is" or fàvçoydé qedéço "he became":

** Accusative

The accusative case is used for the object of a sentence:

    soàzoydé nqem hjopèjodé cyvqedé çosésoqeço = the bad king fears the new generals

It can also be used with a place name to refer to the destination:

    vjohdéyzo séh yntqeso nqecséséço = the magistrate returned to the city

** Genitive

A genitive noun can represent a possessor or a kin:

    zosétnsé ryqezozoàqe = the girl's books, the books of the girl

ADJECTIVES
**********

Adjectives, like nouns, have different endings for the different cases, singular and plural. They also differ as to gender, having different forms for masculine, feminine, and neuter. (But masculine and neuter are identical in the genitive, dative, and ablative cases.)

*****
VERBS
*****

Ydypyçyken is a heavily inflected language with largely free word order. Nouns are inflected for number and case; pronouns and adjectives (including participles) are inflected for number, case, and gender; and verbs are inflected for person, number, tense, aspect, voice, and mood. The inflections are often changes in the ending of a word, but can be more complicated, especially with verbs. Thus verbs can take any of over 100 different endings to express different meanings.

* Ydypyçyken conjugation

In linguistics and grammar, conjugation has two basic meanings. One meaning is the creation of derived forms of a verb from basic forms, or principal parts.

The second meaning of the word conjugation is a group of verbs which all have the same pattern of inflections. Thus all those Ydypyçyken verbs which in the present tense have 1st singular -os, 2nd singular -ypà, and infinitive -ypyvz are said to belong to the 1st conjugation, those with 1st singular -zos, 2nd singular -zà and infinitive -zyvz belong to the 2nd conjugation, and so on. The number of conjugations of regular verbs is usually said to be four.

In addition to regular verbs, which belong to one or other of the four regular conjugations, there are also a few irregular verbs, which have a different pattern of endings. The most frequent of these is the verb àoçu, zààz "to be" together with its prefixed derivatives.

There also exist deponent Ydypyçyken verbs, which though active in meaning have endings identical to the passive verbs. Examples in the different conjugations are: (1) uosyvosyv, uosyvypyvyk "to delay", (2) fosiiykhzosyv, fosiiykhzyvyk "to promise", uykàzyvzosyv, uykàzyvzyvyk "to pity" (3) àzemoçosyv, àzemoçyk "to follow", osriykésykàhosyv, osriykésykàhyk "to forget" and yvzépyvzadykosyv, yvzépyvzadyk "to go back", (4) uzenyçykosyv, uzenyçykyvyk "to lie (tell a lie)". Some verbs are semi-deponent, using passive forms for the perfect tenses only. 

* Principal parts

A verb's full paradigm relies on multiple stems. The present indicative active and the present infinitive are both based on the present stem.

It is not possible to infer the stems for other tenses from the present stem. This means that, although the infinitive active form normally shows the verb conjugation, knowledge of several different forms is necessary to be able to confidently produce the full range of forms for any particular verb.

In a dictionary, Ydypyçyken verbs are listed with four "principal parts" (or fewer for deponent and defective verbs), which allow the student to deduce the other conjugated forms of the verbs. These are:

    the first person singular of the present indicative active
    the present infinitive active
    the first person singular of the perfect indicative active
    the supine or, in some grammars, the perfect passive participle, which uses the same stem. (Texts that list the perfect passive participle use the future active participle for intransitive verbs.) Some verbs lack this principal part altogether.

***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Bàrèmigè has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "réjés hvàgègeo" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Bàrèmigè into English.

*****
NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Bàrèmigè nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: réjés "king", réjécjéo "kings". A few nouns, called tqgerérè mrègèmgef ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. lyrèomrérè "a camp", qimmjérérèjé "a letter", gègetmirèjé "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    itojé réjés "the king himself" (masculine)
    itorè réjécigèrè "the queen herself" (feminine)
    itogef hjéqqgef "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as avàfigègeo "master", tgejéré "boy", ajégeo "god", but also some inanimate objects such as làvàrémgeo "garden", jésjérélyimgeo "army", fvào "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -geo or -jéré are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as tgejéqqrè "girl", fgeqijéré "woman", ajérè "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as rèréhvàré "tree", gerého "city", làgefrègèimrèo "kindness", gèrèmivà "nation". Words in the 1st declension like tgejéqqrè ending in -rè are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as tvàjémrè "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -mrèo and -mivà.
    Neuter nouns (apart from olyvàrémgef "a sex worker (of either gender)") all refer to things, such as gèvàfjégè "name", lyvàrétgeo "body", hjéqqgef "war", çjégèjégègef 'poison'.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of neuter nouns always adds the morpheme r-, e.g. hjéqqrè "wars", lyvàrétvàrérè "bodies"; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical. 

* Case

Nouns in Bàrèmigè have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is réjés when it is the subject of a verb, but réjécjéf when it is the object:

    réjés çiajém "the king sees" (nominative case)
    réjécjéf çiajém "(he/she/it) sees the king" (accusative case)

Further cases mean "of" (genitive case), "to/for" (dative case), and "with" (ablative case).

The genitive case is used to express possession. The genitive singular of nouns is formed as follows:

* The genitive singular of masculine and feminine nouns is formed by adding the morpheme i-. The genitive singular of olyvàrémgef, the unusual neuter noun meaning "sex worker," is formed by adding the morpheme h-.
* The genitive singular of plurals is formed by adding the morpheme và-.

The genitive case of plurals is identical to the plural form of the noun in the accusative case.

The dative case is the recipient of benefactive verbs such as gèjéqgeo "to give" and of verbs of saying or giving, such as jéci "to tell":

    réjés gèjéqgeo réjécjéf "the king gives the queen a gift" 
    réjécjéf jéci réjés "the queen tells the king something"

The dative case of singular nouns (regardless of gender) is formed by adding the morpheme và-. The dative plural is formed by adding the morpheme io.

The ablative case is used to indicate movement away from the referent, as in "réjécjéf rèa 'the queen leaves,' or in the context of certain prepositions, such as rèhgeo 'without': rèhgeo réjécjéf 'without the queen.' The singular ablative is formed by adding the morpheme jé- to feminine nouns and the morpheme và- to masculine and neuter nouns. The plural of the ablative is formed by adding the morpheme io-, whatever the gender of the noun.

The locative case indicates location and is formed by adding the morpheme r- to the singular and the morpheme io- to the plural, whatever the gender of the noun. For example, réjés 'king' becomes rérjés 'at the king' and iojés 'at the kings.'

* Use of cases

** Nominative

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

    réjés agelyim = the king leads
    réjés règeaimgeré = the king is heard

It is also used for the complement of a copula verb such as jéom "he is" or jerèlymgeo jéom "he became":

    réjés jerérèm rèjégèjérèo gèvàhio = our king was rèjégèjérèo / rèjégèjérèo was our king
    réjés jerèlymgeo jéom = he was made king / he became king

** Vocative

The vocative case is used when addressing someone:

    xegehjéogèjé fjé, révàfgeqjé réjés, jevàjéageo jejéréiréjé? = do you order me, King révàfgeqgeo, to strike a treaty?

** Accusative

The accusative case is used for the object of a sentence:

    tvàjémrèjé réjécjéf çiajéhgegèm = the poets will see the king
    frèqgeo réjés gèvàçvào agelyjéo mifjém = the bad king fears the new generals

    réjécjéf igèmjéréjejélymgef jéoojé lyréjéajéhrègèm = they believed that the king had been killed

It can also be used with a place name to refer to the destination:

    révàfrèf trévàjejélymgeo jéom = he set out for révàfjé

The accusative is also used after various prepositions (especially those that imply motion towards):

    lyvàgèogeq igè geréhjéf réjéaiim = the magistrate returned to the city

Another use of the accusative is to give a length of time or distance:

    réjécgèrèçim règègèvào ugeigèugejé = he reigned for five years
    ugeigèugejé tjéajéo qvàgècgeo = five foot tall

** Genitive

A genitive noun can represent a possessor or a kin:

    réjécio jeiqirè = the king's daughter, daughter of the king
    qihréi tgejéqqrèjé = the girl's books, the books of the girl

A frequent type of genitive is the partitive genitive, expressing the quantity of something:

The dative case means "to" or "for". It is frequently used with verbs of saying or giving:

    réjéci gègegèmirèmgef jéom = it was announced to the king

* Yqàqojmèq conjugation

In linguistics and grammar, conjugation has two basic meanings. One meaning is the creation of derived forms of a verb from basic forms, or principal parts.

The second meaning of the word conjugation is a group of verbs which all have the same pattern of inflections. Thus all those Yqàqojmèq verbs which in the present tense have 1st singular -x, 2nd singular -àqð, and infinitive -àqtw are said to belong to the 1st conjugation, those with 1st singular -wx, 2nd singular -wð and infinitive -wtw belong to the 2nd conjugation, and so on. The number of conjugations of regular verbs is usually said to be four.

In addition to regular verbs, which belong to one or other of the four regular conjugations, there are also a few irregular verbs, which have a different pattern of endings. The most frequent of these is the verb ðiu, wððw "to be" together with its prefixed derivatives.

There also exist deponent Yqàqojmèq verbs, which though active in meaning have endings identical to the passive verbs. * Principal parts

A verb's full paradigm relies on multiple stems. The present indicative active and the present infinitive are both based on the present stem.

It is not possible to infer the stems for other tenses from the present stem. This means that, although the infinitive active form normally shows the verb conjugation, knowledge of several different forms is necessary to be able to confidently produce the full range of forms for any particular verb.

***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Waþàbacv has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "sdày pefvñàj" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Waþàbacv into English.

NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Waþàbacv nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: sdày "king", sdàmedàj "kings". A few nouns, called darñàsþàþà baþàvbañàn ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. ñéþàjbasþà "a camp", rcbabadàsþàdà "a letter", vñàdabacþàdà "a wedding".

    cdajþà sdàmecvþà "the queen herself" (feminine)

***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Sisuwxor has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "cgeku gulrgozo" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Sisuwxor into English.

*****
NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Sisuwxor nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: cgeku "king", cgehagezo "kings". A few nouns, called jdgocsudxosu wsurwgoè ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. çasuzowcsu "a camp", dxowwgecsuge "a letter", rgojwxosuge "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    xojzoge cgeku "the king himself" (masculine)
    xojzosu cgehaxorsu "the queen herself" (feminine)
    xojzogoè gugeddgoè "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as tlèxorgozo "master", jgogec "boy", tgegozo "god", but also some inanimate objects such as qlcwgozo "garden", gekugecçaxowgozo "army", èlzo "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -gozo or -gec are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as jgogeddsu "girl", ègodxogec "woman", tgesu "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as sucgulc "tree", gocguzo "city", qgoèsurxowsuzo "kindness", rsuwxol "nation". Words in the 1st declension like jgogeddsu ending in -su are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as jlgewsu "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -wsuzo and -wxol.
    Neuter nouns (apart from zoçalcwgoè "a sex worker (of either gender)") all refer to things, such as rlèger "name", çalcjgozo "body", gugeddgoè "war", gigergergoè 'poison'.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of neuter nouns always adds the morpheme su-, e.g. gugeddsu "wars", çalcjgozo "bodies"; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical.

Nouns in Sisuwxor have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is cgeku when it is the subject of a verb, but cgehageè when it is the object:

    cgeku tgoçaxow = the king sees
    cgehageè gixotgew "(he/she/it) sees the king" (accusative case)

Further cases mean "of" (genitive case), "to/for" (dative case), and "with" (ablative case).

The genitive, dative and ablative cases are called the "oblique" cases.

The order in which the cases are given in Sisuwxor grammar books differs from one author to the other.

* Use of cases

** Nominative

The nominative case is used for the subject of an active or a passive verb:

    cgeku sugotxowgoc = the king is heard

It is also used for the complement of a copula verb such as gezow "he is" or nsuçawgozo gezow "he became":

** Vocative

The vocative case is used when addressing someone:

    pgogugezorge ège, clègodge cgeku, nlgetgozo ngecxocge? = do you order me, King clègodgozo, to strike a treaty?

The accusative case is used for the object of a sentence:

***********

* Articles
Okqèramj has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "ogorp èzymjèbob" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. *****

* Number

Most Okqèramj nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: ogorp "king", ogoréorob "kings". A few nouns, called omsèbogqsamq èrqjèrèbèh ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. çqobèrogq "a camp", samèrèrorogqor "a letter", jèbomèramqor "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    amomobor ogorp "the king himself" (masculine)
    amomobq ogoréamjq "the queen herself" (feminine)
    amomobèbèh èzorssèbèh "the war itself" (neuter)

To a certain extent, the genders follow the meanings of the words (for example, winds are masculine, tree-names feminine):

    Masculine nouns include all those referring to males, such as wymèhamjèbob "master", omèborog "boy", worèbob "god", but also some inanimate objects such as uymogèrèbob "garden", orporogçamèrèbob "army", èhymob "custom". Words in the 2nd declension ending in -èbob or -orog are usually masculine.
    Feminine nouns include all those referring to females, such as omèborssq "girl", èhèbsamorog "woman", worq "goddess", but also inanimate or abstract nouns such as qogèzymog "tree", èbogèzob "city", uèbèhqjamèrqob "kindness", jqèramym "nation". Words in the 1st declension like omèborssq ending in -q are usually feminine, with a few exceptions such as omymorèrq "poet". Also feminine are 3rd declension nouns ending in -èrqob and -èramym.

Neuter nouns differ from masculine and feminine in two ways: (1) the plural of neuter nouns always ends in -q, e.g. èzorssq "wars", çymogomymogq "bodies"; (2) the subject (nominative) and object (accusative) cases are identical.

Nouns in Okqèramj have a series of different forms, called cases of the noun, which have different functions or meanings. For example, the word for "king" is ogorp when it is the subject of a verb, but ogoréorèh when it is the object:

***********
DETERMINERS
***********

* Articles
Mehkèfèpà has no definite or indefinite articles. As a result, the noun and adjective "gjmè rizpàwiu" can be translated as either "the good king" or "a good king," depending on the context. In the absence of context, the definite article is typically preferred when translating from Mehkèfèpà into English.

*****
NOUNS
*****

* Number

Most Mehkèfèpà nouns have two numbers, singular and plural: gjmè "king", gjnju "kings". A few nouns, called ymewighmefèh kèhpàkèwicè ("plural only"), although plural in form, have a singular meaning, e.g. éhukègh "a camp", mefèkèkèjghj "a letter", pàwiykèfèhj "a wedding". 

* Gender

Nouns are divided into three genders, known as masculine, feminine, and neuter. The difference is shown in the pronouns and adjectives that refer to them, for example:

    fèyuj gjmè "the king himself" (masculine)
    fèyuh gjnfèpàh "the queen herself" (feminine)
